overview: Three continuation pages of the State Department’s 1943 “List of Papers” for the Wireless Telephone/Radio—Japan decimal file, indexing items 117–157, with numerous blank or omitted numbers. The entries document wartime collection, monitoring, transcription, and circulation of Japanese broadcasts and intercepted radio traffic by U.S. diplomatic posts, the Federal Communications Commission, the Foreign Broadcast Intelligence Service, the Office of War Information, the Navy, and other agencies. Subjects include Radio Tokyo personnel and commentators, economic intelligence, domestic and marine propaganda, Manchuria and the Philippines, Japanese broadcasts from the Netherlands Indies, and communications between Japan and Argentina.

subfiles.title: List of Papers for Wireless Telephone/Radio—Japan, items 117–157
subfiles.about: A departmental register summarizes correspondence, telegrams, reports, and enclosures concerning Japanese radio broadcasts, propaganda, and intercepted communications.
subfiles.summary: The first page indexes diplomatic reporting from Moscow, Kuibyshev, Shanghai, and other sources on monitored Japanese broadcasts, Radio Tokyo announcer Jack Holland, station lists, transcripts, and reports about Manchuria and the Philippines. The second page records an FCC study of Tokyo commentators, the termination of economic broadcast summaries from Chungking, and exchanges concerning the risks of reusing Japanese broadcasts and Japanese transmissions from Makassar. The final page lists Domei and Japan–Argentina intercepts, requests for Far Eastern radio reports, broadcasts about the Philippine constitution, an inquiry into Seiichi Murata, Jakarta radio intercepts, and expanded monitoring of Japanese domestic and marine broadcasting.

interest: The register offers a compact map of the interagency and international system used to monitor Japanese radio during the Second World War. It is especially useful for tracing how broadcast intelligence moved among embassies, the State Department, the FCC, the Foreign Broadcast Intelligence Service, the Navy, the Office of War Information, and the Board of Economic Warfare. Its entries also expose tensions over propaganda practice—particularly the danger of recycling Japanese material—and identify otherwise granular subjects such as individual announcers, regional transmitters, marine broadcasts, and Japan–Argentina radio traffic.
